subject: science
topic: Your memories are reconstructed every time you recall them
angle: Memory retrieval involves a recombination mechanism that allows for successful inferences but also causes source misattributions and false memories, particularly in younger adults.
title: The Reconstruction of Memory

hooks.text: Can you trust the details of your past?
You think you are remembering, but you are reconstructing.
You are trusting memories that your brain has rewritten.
A warm light in a cafe from years ago.
Your brain reconstructs memories every time you recall them.

reveal.headline: The process that helps you make connections also creates false memories.
reveal.body: The same cognitive mechanism used to make successful inferences contributes to the misattribution of reward-context in memory.

explain.headline: Your brain reconstructs information to fill in the gaps.
explain.body: When you retrieve memories, your brain links different pieces of information. This recombination allows for new inferences but also leads to source misattributions and distorted contextual details.

matters.headline: Your recollections may be more like reconstructions than recordings.
matters.body: That may be why you feel certain about the setting of a past event even if the details are actually incorrect. Your brain prioritizes making sense over perfect accuracy.

example.headline: You recall a dinner at a specific cafe.
example.body: You remember the warm light and the way the table felt. You are certain of the atmosphere, but the details were woven together by your brain as you remembered the conversation.

question.headline: How much of your past is a reconstruction?

claims.text: Older adults did not show an increase in source misattributions following successful associative inference, unlike younger adults.
claims.quote: we found that older adults, in contrast to younger adults, did not show an increase in source misattributions following successful associative inference.

claims.text: There was no overall effect of sleep on either accurate or false memories in a meta-analysis of the Deese/Roediger-McDermott paradigm.
claims.quote: the meta-analysis revealed that, whereas there was no overall effect of sleep on either accurate or false memories, the effect of sleep on overall memories was moderated by two constraints.

claims.text: A retrieval mechanism that helps people make successful inferences also contributes to the misattribution of reward-context in memory.
claims.quote: These results suggest that a recombination-related retrieval mechanism that supports successful inference also contributes to the misattribution of reward-context in memory

claims.text: Participants were more susceptible to false memories for contextual details after successful than unsuccessful inferential retrieval, but only when contextual details were probed after the associative inference test.
claims.quote: participants were more susceptible to false memories for contextual details after successful than unsuccessful inferential retrieval, but only when contextual details were probed after the associative inference test.

claims.text: A group's proneness to false memories was associated with reduced representational match between the tested item and all studied items in the visual cortex.
claims.quote: the AV group’s proneness to false memories was associated with ( i ) reduced representational match between the tested item and all studied items in the visual cortex

claims.text: False memories in immediate recognition tests were accompanied by the reduction of verbatim memory retrieval resulting from the impairment of rehearsal.
claims.quote: the occurrence of false memories in immediate recognition test was accompanied by the reduction of verbatim memory retrieval resulting from the impairment of rehearsal.

verdict: The evidence shows that the same cognitive processes used to link different memories to make new connections also contribute to the creation of false memories and distorted contexts.
caveat: The effects of sleep on memory consolidation are highly dependent on specific task features and the number of items in a list.
caption:
Your brain prioritizes making sense over perfect accuracy. 

Research shows that the same cognitive processes used to link memories and make inferences also contribute to the creation of false memories and distorted contexts. The effects of sleep on memory consolidation are highly dependent on specific task features and the number of items in a list.

What is one memory you are certain of today?
